item.title: 3,000 flights cancelled as FAA ground stop chaos stretches into 2nd day
item.description:
The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop lingered into early Saturday morning, with thousands of flights cancelled as airlines played catch-up.

Why it matters: Millions of travelers will find themselves inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades.

Driving the news: As of 5:15 a.m. ET Saturday, nearly 3,300 flights into, out of, or within the United States were already cancelled for the day, per FlightAware.

  • Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays.

Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan.

  • Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American.

Zoom in: The ground stop wreaked havoc on college football in particular, with many schools unable to travel to their game locations.

  • ESPN reported a number of high-profile match-ups were postponed to either late Saturday or Sunday as a result.

What to watch: Whether Congress responds to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for $50 billion in emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
item.description:
The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January.

Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that state officials have warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage.

Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience.

  • Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times.
  • The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that they'll be kicked out because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements.

This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

item.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
item.description:
Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication.

Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance.

Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received.

  • Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work.
  • That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump's Kennedy Center takeover, saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination."
  • In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well.

Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally.

  • The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting, "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems."
  • U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms.
  • The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage.

What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project.

  • She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed.

While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes.

  • "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says.

Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place.

  • "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds.

With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage."

  • Municipal governments in Austin, Texas, and Jacksonville, Florida, among several others, warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted.

What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress."

  • That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access.

The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps.

item.title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
item.description:
A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system.

The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain.

  • That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around).
  • In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks.

By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000.

  • The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips.

What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them."

  • "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds.
  • "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute.

Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory.

  • "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner.
  • "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed."

Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth.

  • Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

item.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
item.description:
Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high.

Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover.

  • Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers.
  • The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices.

The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate.

  • Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say.

  • Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month (see the chart above), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft.
  • A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens.

"The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states.

Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too.

  • The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning.
  • Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states.

With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter.

Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices.

  • "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email.
  • And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks.

Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil.

  • These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more.

What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening.

  • "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note.

The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes.

  • She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports."

item.title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
item.description:
The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence in hospitals and clinics is leading the nation's biggest physicians group to lobby for new legal protections if AI harms patients.

Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software.

  • There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight.
  • The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong.

Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended.

  • The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data.
  • Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states.

Between the lines: The group's push comes as AI clinical tools are flooding the health system, unlocking new efficiencies but giving algorithms increasing power to make decisions like whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug.

  • Legal and medical experts point to the possibility of triage errors, in which AI systems that process clinical histories, vital signs and imaging can misjudge the severity of a case without the attending doctor's knowledge.
  • The AMA also raises the possibility of an AI system making a plausible recommendation for treatment, but with incomplete laboratory results or an outdated diagnoses. In such cases, a physician may be unable to verify the inputs.
  • In cases where a patient is harmed, responsibility should fall on AI manufacturers and vendors — and possibly on health systems that require the AI systems' use — instead of through a medical malpractice claim against the physician, the AMA argues.

Context: There already have been lawsuits around algorithm-driven medical decisions, including a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities.

  • The software developer wasn't held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors.

The big picture: Courts around the country are concluding that companies that design, train and deploy AI systems bear responsibility for what the systems do, said University of California, Davis professor Martin Hilbert, who studies the role of digital information and algorithms in society.

  • Accountability hinges on factors including who shares responsibility when multiple parties build an AI system, how to prove fault inside an opaque model, and what to do when damages surface only after the system is deployed.
  • "Different parties are responsible for different cases, and you can't just hold the end user responsible," he told Axios.
  • The AMA wants to address situations when use of an AI system is mandatory.

What we're watching: The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices.

  • But the agency oversees software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all of the AI in health care.
  • Hospitals generally support putting the onus on developers and vendors for monitoring the systems' performance, saying the "black box" nature of many systems can make it hard to identify flaws.
  • AdvaMed, the trade group representing device makers, is urging the FDA to continue using its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled medical devices. It also wants the agency to avoid post-market monitoring that imposes added burdens regardless of a product's actual risk.

item.title: The AI boom will survive without Jensen Huang, but there's a $500 billion funding hole to fill
item.description:
The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook.

Why it matters: With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia.

  • But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder.

The big picture: The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons:

1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain.

  • At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer.
  • The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI, as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever.
  • AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days, compared with six to 12 months in the past.

2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales.

  • Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access.
  • Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI.

Reality check: Alternative chips and leaps forward in software won't solve the near-term computing crunch that all the big players in AI are facing.

  • Nvidia's chips remain the most sought-after because they are the most widely supported, making them critical for the industry's smaller players and important for the big companies who need maximum efficiency out of each data center they build.

There are two reasons a strong Nvidia still remains essential:

1. Finance - The company's checkbook will be far more difficult to replicate than its computing power.

  • Nvidia has made $530 billion of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees, including to buy memory and backstops for data centers and certain companies building them, according to data firm SemiAnalysis.
  • Smaller cloud providers, often called neoclouds, as well as a vast array of startups all over the world, have lost perhaps their most enthusiastic champion.
  • Nvidia will remain a formidable competitor, but it will almost certainly become less aggressive about startup funding, acquisitions and backstops, tempering its efforts to spread exposure among institutional investors in ways that some critics said resembled the mortgage bubble.

2. Open models - Nvidia has been the most enthusiastic funder and champion of the Western open-model ecosystem—giving developers cheaper alternatives to the expensive offerings from frontier AI companies.

  • Its pending acquisition of Hugging Face, licensing agreement with model-developer Poolside, backing of Reflection and development of the Nemotron family of open models extend well beyond chip sales.
  • Without Nvidia, it's not clear whether the U.S. will be able to develop open-weight alternatives to China, since many don't have a clear or easy path to financial returns given that such systems are often free to download.

What we're watching: Whether the industry's growing freedom to choose its chips can compensate for an Nvidia that is suddenly much less willing to finance its ambitions.

Bottom line: Huang's departure won't derail America's AI ambitions. But it leaves a hole in the ecosystem that will be harder to fill than any shortage of Nvidia chips.

The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook.

Why it matters: With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia.

  • But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder.

The big picture: The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons:

1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain.

  • At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer.
  • The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI, as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever.
  • AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days, compared with six to 12 months in the past.

2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales.

  • Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access.
  • Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI.

Reality check: Alternative chips and leaps forward in software won't solve the near-term computing crunch that all the big players in AI are facing.

  • Nvidia's chips remain the most sought-after because they are the most widely supported, making them critical for the industry's smaller players and important for the big companies who need maximum efficiency out of each data center they build.

There are two reasons a strong Nvidia still remains essential:

1. Finance - The company's checkbook will be far more difficult to replicate than its computing power.

  • Nvidia has made $530 billion of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees, including to buy memory and backstops for data centers and certain companies building them, according to data firm SemiAnalysis.
  • Smaller cloud providers, often called neoclouds, as well as a vast array of startups all over the world, have lost perhaps their most enthusiastic champion.
  • Nvidia will remain a formidable competitor, but it will almost certainly become less aggressive about startup funding, acquisitions and backstops, tempering its efforts to spread exposure among institutional investors in ways that some critics said resembled the mortgage bubble.

2. Open models - Nvidia has been the most enthusiastic funder and champion of the Western open-model ecosystem—giving developers cheaper alternatives to the expensive offerings from frontier AI companies.

  • Its pending acquisition of Hugging Face, licensing agreement with model-developer Poolside, backing of Reflection and development of the Nemotron family of open models extend well beyond chip sales.
  • Without Nvidia, it's not clear whether the U.S. will be able to develop open-weight alternatives to China, since many don't have a clear or easy path to financial returns given that such systems are often free to download.

What we're watching: Whether the industry's growing freedom to choose its chips can compensate for an Nvidia that is suddenly much less willing to finance its ambitions.

Bottom line: Huang's departure won't derail America's AI ambitions. But it leaves a hole in the ecosystem that will be harder to fill than any shortage of Nvidia chips.

item.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
item.description:
Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse.

  • The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure.

  • The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure.

Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor, leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm.

  • In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company.

Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots.

Colette Kress

Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page

Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters. Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers.

  • Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives.
  • She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business.

Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess.

Ian Buck

Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets

Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia.

  • He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing.
  • He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development.

Chris Malachowsky

Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets

Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page.

  • "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads.
  • Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership.

Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position.

René Haas

Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports.

  • He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes.
  • Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products.

Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition.

Tim Cook

President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images

Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia.

  • Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse.
  • Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation.

Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO.

Johny Srouji

Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Bloomberg has identified Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor.

  • Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices.

Nikesh Arora

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name.

  • Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity.
  • He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography.

Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development.

Lisa Su

AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry.

Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, and she was just named "CEO of the Year" by Yahoo! Finance.

  • Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried says Su might relish competing with a weakened Nvidia rather than taking over for Huang.

Thomas Kurian

Thomas Kurian speaks onstage during Oracle's OpenWorld conference in San Francisco in 2017. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud could also be considered.

  • Kurian oversees cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience with major customers and technology essential to Nvidia's business.

Yes, but: His resume does not feature chip design experience.

Pat Gelsinger

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger holds up a processor while speaking onstage at the Computex technology conference in Taipei in 2024. Photo: Annabelle Chih/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The former Intel CEO boasts decades of semiconductor engineering and leadership experience at one of Nvidia's longtime competitors.

  • Gelsinger has publicly criticized Nvidia's approach to AI computing, backed its competitors and sparred with Huang over the future of chips.

Yes, but: Gelsinger struggled to make Intel a stronger AI competitor. His name has surfaced in online speculation, but there's no public indication Nvidia's board is considering him.

Madison Huang

Nvidia executives Madison Huang (left) and Spencer Huang attend a company event at the site of Nvidia's planned Constellation campus in Taipei in May 2026. Photo: An Rong Xu/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Huang's daughter Madison has emerged as a possible long-term successor, according to reporting by the Financial Times, citing sources familiar.

  • She's a senior director working on product marketing for Nvidia's physical AI business and has been described as a rising star within the company. Her name has also surfaced in prediction market speculation.

Zoom in: Huang's son Spencer and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia. Caprez, who oversees global AI infrastructure growth, has also been tapped as a potential successor, per Bloomberg.

Yes, but: Huang's children hold relatively junior positions compared with Nvidia's more experienced executives.

  • Asked about his daughter's potential succession in the Bloomberg interview, Huang said Madison and her brother Spencer would have to earn the position rather than inherit it.

item.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
item.description:
Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself.

Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise.

The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap.

  • "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios.

Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including:

What will the investigations uncover?

  • Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences.
  • Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee.

Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public.

  • Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it.
  • Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter.

Who takes the permanent role as CEO?

  • CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally and we are big fans of her strategically," tech bull Dan Ives wrote Thursday in a research note.
  • Prediction markets point to Nvidia hyperscaling tech exec Ian Buck as the the leading candidate, but the political ramifications of Nvidia's position in the global economy may demand someone with more experience with geopolitics.
  • President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook, whom Ives also floated, but Kalshi traders rate that as a 1 in 25 shot.

Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble?

  • Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars — and Huang is at the center of that vast flywheel, Axios' Zachary Basu writes.

Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says.

  • "This Nvidia story is going to take a little air out of the balloon for the Anthropic IPO," he says.

The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips:

  • "The company was never the source of AI demand. It has been supplying the capacity to meet that demand," which remains "enormous," he wrote today.

Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry?

  • Competitors like AMD, Alphabet and Intel could benefit if chips customers are soured on working with Nvidia.
  • "When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: did the clients sign with the banker — or with the bank? Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market," writes Mark Malek, CIO at Siebert Financial.

What's the floor for Nvidia's stock?

  • Nvidia shares were down another 5.7% just before 3pm Thursday and are now down 27% over the last month, having lost about $1 trillion in value.
  • "With this kind of leadership uncertainty, it's very difficult to predict where shares go over the next several trading sessions," writes Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. "Sometimes huge news catalysts like this take all technicals out of the equation."

The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang?

  • Elon Musk has already hinted he could hire the former Nvidia chief as he moves toward a possible merger of SpaceX and Tesla.
  • But it'll be hard for anyone to hire Huang unless and until the FBI probe in particular is resolved.

The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

item.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it.

Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign.

  • But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight.
  • That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy.

What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday.

Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month.

  • Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs.
  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%.
  • Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June.

The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace.

  • The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May.
  • The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI, which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025.
  • More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X.

Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation.

  • Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates.
  • Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates.
  • Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning.

What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing.

  • President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border.
  • Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran, raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

  • More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X.

  • Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates.
  • Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates.
  • Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning.

What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing.

  • President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border.
  • Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran, raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

item.description:

item.title: Jensen Huang, an architect of the AI boom, resigns as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy.

Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy.

  • His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble.
  • It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself.

Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement.

  • Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company.
  • Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair.
  • The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

What they're saying: "I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy," Kress said in a note to staff after the news came out.

  • "We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company," she added.

Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships.

  • The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him.
  • Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset.
  • Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO.

By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell as much as 13% after news of Huang's resignation before rebounding somewhat.

  • One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang.

🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history.

  • Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index funds because of its size, meaning this move has massive implications for every American with a retirement account.

The intrigue: Huang's resignation doesn't look like it'll ease congressional pressure over his behavior either.

  • "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement.

The bottom line: The fallout is just starting.

This is breaking news.

item.title: Jensen Huang's ouster triggers an AI earthquake
item.description:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023.

Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars.

  • At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution.
  • "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X, warning of contagion across the AI industry.

The latest: Huang resigned from all his positions at Nvidia, the company's board of directors said Thursday, following allegations of two affairs, including one with a woman accused of being a spy for China.

  • The board named Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable.

  • Even after his affair with Alice Huang — the woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive.
  • It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Jensen Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end.

Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate. The White House was read in.

  • The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight.
  • One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang.

Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history.

  • Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution.
  • Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders.

The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.

  • The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic, whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade.
  • Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist.

What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China.

  • Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling.
  • Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation.

The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with news of Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia.

item.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent fall from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create.

Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia.

  • Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy.

Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

  • The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang.
  • Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session.

Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years.

  • The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers.
  • Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth.
  • There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle.
  • "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness."

Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session.

Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios.

  • With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100.

Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is.

  • It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman.
  • It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power.
  • That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds.
  • For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI.

Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers.

  • In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day.

State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement.

  • On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research.
  • "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
  • Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month.

What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis.

  • "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions."

The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history.

  • From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet.
  • He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993.

The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

item.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
item.description:
President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.

  • One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal.

  • This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions.

Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

  • During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent.
  • Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president."

Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen.

  • "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit.
  • "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another.

This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?"

  • Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office.
  • Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China."
  • "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said.

Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic.

  • "I'll develop some options and come back," he said.
  • "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened."

The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations.

Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.

  • But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward.
  • In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials.
  • In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing."

item.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.

Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it."

  • Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings.
  • But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary."
  • Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China.
  • Spokespeople for Treasury couldn't be immediately reached for comment.

The other side: The Commerce Department denied the Situation Room confrontation occurred.

  • "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation," spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said.

Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio.

  • Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported.
  • On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened.
  • The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so.

Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday.

  • "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting.
  • Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it."
  • One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed.

The big picture: Nvidia's AI chips provide the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including systems that could transform warfare and cyberattacks.

Between the lines: The rivalry between Bessent and Lutnick dates to Trump's transition, when both sought the Treasury secretary job. After Trump chose Bessent, the two clashed over trade policy.

  • Bessent's confrontation comes amid a broader slowdown in Commerce's enforcement of U.S. export restrictions, with national security officials increasingly frustrated by decisions to avoid antagonizing China.
  • Blacklisting a company is an interagency decision, with Commerce leading a committee that includes State, Defense and Energy, and consults Treasury when appropriate.
  • Commerce has not added a single company to its Entity List in more than a year, according to a review of the Federal Register, despite mounting pressure from national security officials.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: The AI industry's week from hell
item.description:
A week of political upheaval, financial turmoil and salacious scandal delivered one final indignity to the AI industry Tuesday, as Anthropic's staggering IPO target fell short of expectations.

Why it matters: The bubble is wobbling. Investors, businesses and governments need a spectacular success from Anthropic to stave off a crisis of confidence that could tear through the broader economy.

  • Facing new political headwinds, the industry can scarcely afford another setback — much less the spectacle of AI's crown jewel losing its luster on Wall Street.

Zoom in: Anthropic announced plans Tuesday to raise as much as $64.4 billion in one of the largest IPOs in history, targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

  • That's roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago, as slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a punishing market selloff tempered expectations.
  • Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have also climbed to nearly $901 billion.

Zoom out: Anthropic's valuation reset caps a punishing stretch of new challenges that began with last week's stunning midterm results:

🌊 A blue wave of AI-skeptical Democrats will arrive in Congress armed with subpoena power and an appetite for investigating the industry's safety failures and vast political influence.

  • Voters delivered another blow at the local level, favoring restrictions on data-center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide.

🤖 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central cog in AI's global gears, was swept up in an espionage scandal after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. His board, the FBI and Congress are investigating.

  • Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times revelations on Oct. 29, with shares plunging further Tuesday as the company faces a new shareholder lawsuit.

📉 Wall Street went into a tailspin as investors reckoned with the implications of the Democratic sweep — including in data-center havens like Texas — for AI's sprawling infrastructure ambitions.

  • The Nasdaq lost $2.5 trillion in market value Thursday, its worst session since April 2025, before staging a sharp rebound.

⚠️ Financial warning signs are mounting: OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions, while SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment, contributing to a $7 billion quarterly loss.

  • Amid renewed fears of rate hikes, anxiety is also spreading to credit markets, where lenders have grown wary of financing the industry's astronomical infrastructure spending.

Reality check: Anthropic is still poised for one of the largest IPOs ever, with Google, Nvidia and other technology giants committing another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering.

  • The company could emerge with roughly $85 billion in net new capital — a historic financial windfall for a company founded less than six years ago.

Yes, but: Bubbles don't run on "good enough." They demand more, better and faster — indefinitely.

  • Even a $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion valuation of Anthropic may not be enough to reassure investors, who thought just a few weeks ago it'd be worth as much as $2 trillion.

What to watch: Whether Anthropic can deliver a spectacular debut and sustain it after trading begins. SpaceX's stock surged after its record June IPO, only to surrender those gains and fall below its offering price within weeks.

item.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
item.description:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities.

Driving the news: Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times.

  • The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's May 13–15 trip to China.
  • Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday.
  • On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips.
  • Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers.

Yes, but: It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals.

  • Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets.

What they're saying: Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me."

  • The Commerce Department did not comment.

Catch up quick: Nvidia has been rocked by the scandal, losing about $1 trillion in market value since the Times' first reported the relationship, although some of that decline also came after an overwhelming number of Democrats promising to slow an AI data-center buildout were elected in the midterms.

  • Huang acknowledged an affair Sunday, and Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation. The board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security secrets were compromised.

What to watch: New revelations continue to drop almost daily about the administration's handling of the Nvidia CEO's relationship. Lawmakers in both parties have promised investigations and demanded more information, including closed-door testimony from Jensen Huang next week.

  • Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs committee have also demanded answers from Lutnick about the administration's chip approvals, "including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang."

item.title: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
item.description:
Federal Reserve Bank of New York; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals

Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally.

By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier.

  • The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms.
  • Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic.

Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments.

  • The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic.

Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts.

  • Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022.
  • In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods.

The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now $6,678, according to TransUnion's Q3 insights report.

  • Borrowers under 30 had the highest rate of credit card debt newly becoming at least 90 days overdue, the Fed's report found.

What we're watching: Democrats won the midterms promising to lower prices — but delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets will be difficult to fulfill.

item.title: Harsh new inflation reality
item.description:
America's inflation problem is stubborn, broadening out and showing no sign of letting up.

Why it matters: October marked the third straight month of hotter-than-expected inflation, defying repeated predictions over the last couple of years that price pressures were finally about to ease.

  • In this sixth consecutive year of steep price increases, consumers are finding there is nowhere to hide from inflation.
  • The Iran war has added to the pain, but other factors — tariffs and the AI investment boom — have also put upward pressure on costs, complicating an affordability problem that long predates the conflict.

What they're saying: "Today's inflation report is a warning shot," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, wrote Tuesday morning.

  • "Coming just a week after the midterm elections exposed the depth of voters' concerns about affordability, the message for the Fed is uncomfortable but clear: The inflation fight is not finished," Shah wrote.

Driving the news: The headline Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, down slightly from a 0.6% surge the previous month.

  • Core CPI — which excludes volatile food and energy costs — climbed 0.3% for the third consecutive month, a sign that underlying inflationary pressures remain stubbornly persistent.

The Labor Department did not calculate October's annual inflation rate since last year's government shutdown prevented it from collecting price data for October 2025.

  • But assuming prices that month were halfway between September and November, overall inflation over the last 12 months was 4% — up from 3.7% in September. Core inflation would have risen to 2.8%, up from 2.6%.
  • Another measure similarly paints a picture of hot inflation. Core prices rose at a 3.7% annualized pace over the three months through October, the fastest pace by this gauge all year.
  • It also is a sharp acceleration from the summer, when underlying inflation appeared to be cooling.

Zoom out: Gasoline prices advanced another 1% in October after surging 9.1% in September, adding to the steep increase in fuel costs since the Iran war began.

  • Food prices climbed, raising concerns that higher diesel costs are rippling through to consumer prices. Grocery prices increased 0.4% after declining in September, while restaurant prices gained 0.5%.
  • Shelter costs rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the overall increase in consumer prices last month.

Zoom in: Inflation is persistent in the services sector, which is largely insulated from swings in energy prices.

  • A closely watched inflation measure that excludes housing, energy and food prices surged 0.4% in October — pushed up by higher costs in transportation, medical care and insurance.

What to watch: A strong labor market is not providing much relief from the sharply rising cost of living.

  • Inflation has now outpaced or matched wage growth for three consecutive months, leaving workers with less purchasing power.

item.title: Price pressures persisted in October
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation remained hot in October, according to data from the Labor Department released on Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Consumer Price Index shows that even as gasoline prices steadied, inflation pressures elsewhere remained stubborn.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.4% last month, slowing from the 0.6% increase in September.

  • Gasoline prices gained 1% in October, a sharp slowdown from the 9.1% surge in September, the Labor Department said.
  • Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, advanced 0.3% for the third straight month, with higher prices for recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares contributing to the increase.

Of note: The Labor Department did not publish year-over-year inflation rates for October. Last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data that prevents direct comparisons with October 2025.

  • But if one assumes the October 2025 readings were halfway between September and November, year-over-year inflation comes to 4% — or 2.8% excluding food and energy.
  • That compares with September's annual inflation rate of 3.7%, or 2.6% excluding food and energy.

The big picture: The inflation report was already shaping up to be a crucial piece of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next month. But the stakes grew just hours before its release when Fed governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual rate hike if inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

  • In a speech, Fed governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate hike should be considered next month if core inflation rose by at least 0.3% in October — exactly what Tuesday's report showed.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rate policy, jumped 0.13% on Tuesday following Waller's comments and the CPI report.

What to watch: The report also offers a fresh measure of the inflation problem that helped shape last week's midterm elections.

  • Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote in last week's midterms, according to national exit polling data.
  • Democrats won on promises to lower prices for groceries and other essentials. Now they face the more difficult task of delivering on their promises, with limited power to reverse years of price increases.

The bottom line: Inflation remains stubbornly hot, strengthening the case for another Fed rate hike and prolonging the cost-of-living pressures that have frustrated American households.
