item.title: The path ahead for the permitting bill
item.description:
The Senate's bipartisan permitting bill advanced in a lopsided vote on Monday, but key hurdles lie ahead.

Why it matters: The legislation could have far-reaching consequences for how energy projects get built across the U.S.

A few takeaways from Monday's vote:

The big margin was politically lopsided. The 73-25 split to advance the bill "was as good or a little bit better" than what co-author Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) was expecting, she told reporters in the Capitol.

  • The GOP split was 51-1 in favor, with only Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) voting no.
  • 21 Democrats and Maine independent Sen. Angus King voted yes, while 23 Dems and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders were against advancing the bill toward full debate.

It was tentative. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement afterward that he has "outstanding concerns" with the bill that he'll "fight to address" through amendments.

  • He's not alone in only a tentative yes vote. For instance, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) is against final passage unless changes to the National Historic Preservation Act are jettisoned, citing tribal concerns.
  • Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) is in a similar place.

Climate hawk vs. climate hawk. The most outspoken Senate Democrats on climate change split on the vote.

  • Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) joined coauthors Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) in backing the measure.
  • But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.), along with Sanders, all voted no.

Watch the clock. Whitehouse pledged a "very healthy" amendment process. But the Senate is now up against the lame duck calendar, and the House would still need to act on whatever emerges.

  • Plus, any changes would need to thread a political needle of maintaining Democratic support without losing too many Republicans.

Climate's cachet has fallen. Heinrich and Whitehouse, at a pre-vote press conference, emphasized affordability, data center accountability and jobs before touting power sector emissions curbs from the bill.

  • But Whitehouse also sought to reassure climate and environmental organizations.
  • "This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations, and we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities," he said in the Capitol.

President Trump is a wild card. His comments shortly before Monday's vote that he would not approve wind turbines, while reiterating his full support for the bill, rocketed around the Capitol.

  • And the White House reaffirmed that the president "stands 100%" behind the bill.
  • The bill's success depends on Trump officials "getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid," and progress is needed before final passage, Whitehouse said in a statement.

What we're watching: Proposed amendments as they roll in, but also the politics in the closely divided House.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) criticized the bill last week and called for more engagement with his caucus.
  • Asked Monday whether the Senate co-authors' revisions addressed his concerns, Jeffries told reporters that it's still under review.

item.title: How Nvidia's crisis and politics could deliver the pause AI leaders want
item.description:
A political backlash against AI and data centers — now compounded by a crisis facing the technology's most influential champion — could help force a slowdown that industry leaders have struggled to achieve voluntarily.

Why it matters: Tapping the brakes on AI development — which frontier AI developers claim to want but have so far failed to do given the risk of offering an advantage to a competitor — could give society more time to prepare for economic upheaval and the risks of superintelligent systems.

  • A wave of Democratic victories and data center moratoriums is now joined by a potentially weakened Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
  • Huang, who has led the industry in barreling through past resistance to AI acceleration, may be less able to do so while under a microscope.
  • While both factors could stymie data center expansion in the U.S., it's far from clear that would slow AI's advance.

Between the lines: Huang has been a powerful counterweight to calls for AI restraint, dismissing fears of an AI bubble or purported catastrophic risks to humanity from the technology.

  • An investigation — by the board, an ascendant Democratic Congress or federal authorities — could curb his ability to make the case for continued expansion, leaving an opening for those calling for more restrictions.
  • Nvidia says Huang will remain CEO and the news won't slow the company, but the potential impact on his political influence is hard to measure.
  • The fallout extends beyond that. Nvidia is both the dominant supplier of AI chips and an investor in companies building AI infrastructure. A crisis that raises questions about its leadership, business practices or financial relationships could ripple through the industry's expansion plans.

The intrigue: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all warned about the potentially catastrophic risks of advanced AI, with all expressing, at times, the need to slow or pace the development of advanced AI.

  • But the competitive race has made it difficult for any one company to hit the brakes without risking falling behind rivals or China in a high-stakes race for supremacy.

What they're saying: Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, says a slowdown in data center construction would be welcome, even if it wouldn't accomplish nearly as much as more direct restrictions on frontier AI development.

  • "I'll take whatever I can get," Aguirre told Axios in an interview. Aguirre and a number of other researchers have long seen the development of increasingly powerful AI as an existential threat.
  • But he is skeptical that slowing data center construction alone would buy society an additional year or two, given the vast computing resources companies already possess and the growing ability of AI systems to help improve themselves.
  • Aguirre said the bigger opportunity may be political: Resistance to data centers could help generate momentum for legislation and regulation that more directly limits the development of potentially dangerous AI systems.

The big picture: Aguirre argues that the goal shouldn't simply be to delay superintelligence by a year or two, but to reconsider whether humanity should build it at all.

  • He favors a "pause and pivot" toward AI systems designed to augment human abilities rather than replace them.
  • Other researchers and executives favor continued development with stronger safeguards, reflecting a broader debate over how much restraint is necessary and what form it should take.

Yes, but: Slowing data center construction in the U.S. doesn't necessarily mean slowing AI progress globally.

  • Meta and other companies are exploring data center construction outside the U.S. Google announced a plan last week to invest $15 billion over two years in Malaysia.
  • And Chinese AI developers wouldn't face the same U.S. restrictions, potentially allowing them to narrow the gap with American competitors.

The other side: The threat from China isn't as straightforward as it appears.

  • Chinese AI companies benefit in part from distillation of leading American models and technical knowledge developed in the U.S., Aguirre said. Slowing the American frontier could therefore have some effect on China's pace as well.
  • A U.S. decision to slow frontier development could open the door to direct conversations with China about mutually pacing the technology, rather than treating superintelligence as an unavoidable arms race.

The bottom line: The AI industry is hoping to overcome political resistance and keep building. Advocates of slowing frontier AI see an opportunity to turn that resistance into something bigger: a chance to reconsider not just how fast AI should advance, but how far it should go.

item.title: AI stocks bounce back — with one notable exception
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang.

The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom.

By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year.

Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception.

  • Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared.
  • The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.)
  • Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%.
  • Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July.

Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia.

  • Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future.

The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals.

  • Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year.
  • Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday.

Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch.

  • "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday.
  • "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night.
  • "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday.

These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips.

  • And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors.

The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off.

  • For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat.
  • Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors.

What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance?

  • Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce?

item.title: France says Iranian hackers sabotaged supermarket refrigerators
item.description:
The French government has blamed an Iranian military hacking unit for cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 grocery stores and other retail locations last month, causing food losses and at least 15 fires.

Why it matters: The attacks underscore how Iranian government hackers are moving beyond stealing data and disrupting websites to manipulating the physical equipment that keeps essential services running.

Driving the news: France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs attributed the Oct. 11–12 attacks to Iran on Monday, calling them the country's first cyberattack campaign conducted purely for sabotage on French territory.

  • The government's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center specifically attributed the attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
  • Hackers manipulated refrigeration equipment to raise temperatures, causing tens of millions of euros in food losses and at least 15 fires, according to French officials.
  • The same operation also targeted equipment at small hydroelectric facilities in France, with limited effects, according to an intelligence report.

Yes, but: The French government has not publicly attributed a separate wave of refrigeration attacks that occurred last week to the same hackers.

Zoom in: French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to several online hacktivist personas, including CyberAveng3rs and Soldiers of Solomon, that publicly claim responsibility for the unit's operations.

  • Investigators found that infrastructure used in the refrigeration attacks was also used to scan industrial equipment using techniques previously associated with Shahid Kaveh.
  • They also found traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure and identified a propaganda outlet linked to the unit that publicized the attack.

The big picture: Iran has a history of targeting industrial equipment in cyber operations, including American water systems and Israeli refrigeration equipment.

  • French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to attacks on Israeli refrigeration equipment earlier this year and a 2023 campaign targeting industrial controllers manufactured by Unitronics.

What to watch: France plans to summon Iran's ambassador and propose new European Union sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities involved in the attacks.

item.title: What we know about the mystery woman at the center of Nvidia's spy scandal
item.description:
Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair.

Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race.

Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • Though he did not name Alice Huang, the letter came after The New York Times first reported that U.S. authorities believed she was a Chinese spy in October.
  • Photos captured Alice and Jensen Huang together in 2024 and 2025.
  • Though they have the same surname, Alice and Jensen Huang are not related or married. Jensen Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years.

Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer.

  • The New York Times reported Monday that the Commerce Department was leading the investigation into Megaspeed before it was sent to the Justice Department after Nvidia reached out about the case.

Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below.

Who is Alice Huang?

Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance.

  • An AFP investigation found an online profile that said she previously worked at the financial services company HSBC and the broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV.
  • However, AFP said it couldn't independently verify the information.

Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms.

  • But it's still unclear what information she provided to Beijing and whether she obtained any from Jensen Huang.
  • Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe Alice Huang obtained trade secrets. China has also denied the allegations.

What to know about Alice Huang's company

Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips.

  • Before it was Megaspeed, the company was known as 7Road International, a subsidiary of prominent Chinese video game developer, 7Road Holdings. Before the AI boom, Nvidia products were primarily used in the video game industry.
  • In the 2010s, Alice worked at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, which had investment connections to the 7Road gaming company. She also sold a cloud business to 7Road in 2019, according to documents compiled by Tesari AI, an AI startup focused on national security matters.
  • 7Road International, the Singapore subsidiary of 7Road Holdings, became Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became managing director, per Tesari AI's documents. Her company Huang Le Limited became the sole owner of Megaspeed.

In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata. Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company.

  • The company faced an investigation by Singapore police in October 2025 over violations of local laws, but specific offenses were not shared publicly.

Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning.

  • Alice Huang is "actually still our boss," an employee told Culper Research, which published an investigation into Nvidia's China business in May 2026.

How Alice Huang's Megaspeed ties to Nvidia

By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg, and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP.

  • Alice Huang bragged about her access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia connections to help raise funds for her businesses, according to the NYT.
  • A Megaspeed employee told Culper that Jensen Huang would visit Megaspeed sometimes, adding that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship.

Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline.

  • Much of that growth involved approximately $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an unidentified source, per Culper.
  • The financing raises additional questions about Megaspeed's relationship with Chinese businesses.

More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times.

What are authorities investigating?

State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated export-control restrictions.

  • The company disputed illegal chip transfers in December 2025. The company has said it plans to work with U.S. authorities over the investigation.

What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Jensen Huang on Nov. 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign threats.

item.title: Nvidia has no obvious successor to Jensen Huang — and that's a problem
item.description:
Nvidia is coming under fire for having no clear succession plan to replace Jensen Huang in the event that something unexpected happens — like an international incident with him at the center.

Why it matters: The spotlight on Huang shows the vulnerabilities of a large company being dependent on one executive — and the risks it poses to investors and customers, corporate governance experts tell Axios.

Catch up quick: Huang — who founded the chips giant, serves as its all-powerful CEO and exerts significant influence over the global AI economy — admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

  • Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation Sunday, and experts say Huang's chances of keeping his job are a coin flip.

The big picture: The company, by all accounts, has no clear bench of potential replacements.

  • Huang famously has dozens of direct reports, ensuring that no single individual — other than him — has a wide-ranging purview at the company.

"The biggest issue is no human goes on forever, and this is exactly why you want a good succession plan in place if something like this were to happen," says Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert and former University of Delaware professor.

  • "You can't base a company that big around one person. You just can't," Elson added. "What if he gets hit by a bus?"
  • CEO succession planning is a standard practice for big public companies, and it's not clear whether Nvidia has a confidential plan.

State of play: The highest-profile member of Huang's executive team is Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, who appears alongside him during the company's earnings calls.

  • But analysts say Kress — who has spent her career in financial roles — isn't necessarily a natural successor to Huang in his role as an innovator and visionary for the AI age.

What they're saying: "It's ridiculous that they have nobody in management identified," says Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor at the Yale School of Management who is one of the nation's premier CEO whisperers. And no one has been put through any kind of trial assignments to get them ready for the role, Sonnenfeld says.

  • The lack of a clear succession plan suggests Nvidia's board was "asleep at the wheel," says Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University.
  • Consequently, it's essential that the board now steps up and exerts its authority by ensuring that the investigation is thorough, independent, and "reveals as much as they can," Jaworski says. "Transparency is really critical."

For now, Nvidia investors are anxiously awaiting results of the probe — but in general, most say they are hoping he's able to stay.

  • "In some ways he's irreplaceable," says Michael Monaghan, partner at Founder ETFs, an Nvidia investor.
  • Monaghan says Founder ETFs — which specializes in backing founder-led companies — will sell Nvidia shares if Huang exits.
  • "We don't really believe there is such thing as succession in these massive founder-led companies," Monaghan says.

Reality check: There are many examples of companies surviving and even thriving after a well-known headline-grabbing founder departs — think Travis Kalanick at Uber.

  • "People thought he was so critical," says Sonnenfeld. The company did "far better when they got rid of him."

Yes, but: Nvidia might not have a choice.

  • "We always think there's no chance this person gets fired, until they do – and this might be one of those cases," Georgetown's Jaworski says.

Nvidia reps had no immediate comment.

What we're watching: Sonnenfeld says that he's heard former Google CEO Eric Schmidt's name come up as someone who could steer the company if Huang has to step away.

  • "I've heard it rumored. He could step in tomorrow and do a very good job," Sonnenfeld says.

item.title: Low unemployment, but job worries persist
item.description:
Americans have conflicting views of the job market: They are more worried about unemployment rising nationwide, even as they are more confident that they could find another job if they lost their own.

Driving the news: The perceived probability that unemployment will rise over the next year climbed to 45.3% in October, the highest since April 2020, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations — an increase driven by those without a college degree.

Yes, but: The perceived probability of finding another job if one lost their current position rose to 46.5%, the highest in about a year.

  • Americans' perceived probability of losing their jobs over the next year also edged higher, rising 0.4 percentage point, to 13.9%.

State of play: The mixed outlook underscores an unusual feature of today's labor market — hiring is picking up and unemployment remains historically low, but finding work can still be a prolonged struggle.

The backdrop: The October jobs report showed that employers added a surprisingly robust 165,000 jobs last month. The unemployment rate has held in the narrow range of 4% to 4.2% for five consecutive months.

  • But Friday's data also showed that 2 million Americans have been unemployed for at least six months, accounting for more than 25% of all unemployed workers.
  • The average spell of unemployment climbed to 27.1 weeks in October, the longest since December 2021. (Excluding the pandemic, it's the highest reading since August 2016.)

Of note: Ahead of the October Consumer Price Index report — out tomorrow — the New York Fed said that inflation expectations were unchanged last month at 3.9% over the next year, 3.3% over three years and 3% over five years.

item.title: Oil prices and bond yields no longer moving together
item.description:
Data: Axios analysis of FactSet data; Note: Correlation over preceding 30 trading sessions between daily change in West Texas Intermediate crude and change in 10-year U.S. Treasury yield; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

For much of this year, on any given day, you could look at the price of oil and correctly guess what happened to bond yields. In the last few weeks, that correlation has evaporated.

Why it matters: It's a sign that growth risks may be supplanting inflation worries as the dominant economic concern.

State of play: It's not obvious whether an energy supply shock should affect inflation or growth more.

  • On the one hand, more expensive fuel can ripple through prices for everything else. On the other, more expensive energy acts like a tax on consumers and businesses that consume it.
  • Since the attack on Iran in late February, markets have treated the former concern as the central dynamic in the global economy.

Zoom in: As such, on days when oil futures pointed to higher prices, bonds almost always sold off and their yields — which move in the opposite direction from their prices — rose.

  • Traders were pricing in a world where inflation is higher for longer, and central banks react by raising rates more — and betting, implicitly, that growth would prove resilient despite the energy price headwind.
  • For the 30 trading days ended Sept. 10, the correlation between the one-day move in West Texas Intermediate crude and 10-year U.S. Treasury yield reached a stunning 77%.
  • The Financial Times noted in late September that the correlation was the highest it had been since the Persian Gulf War of the early 1990s.

Yes, but: Now, that correlation has collapsed — and is about negative 10% over the last 30 trading days. In other words, on days when oil rises, it's more likely than not that bond yields fall.

Between the lines: It's probably not a coincidence that this shift has occurred at the same time cracks have appeared in the debt market that's financing the AI buildout.

  • As long as the AI and data center boom was powering ahead, seemingly impervious to energy price shocks or bubble fears, the inflationary impact of higher oil prices dominated the economic outlook.
  • But with that sector wobbling, the economy may be more vulnerable to a growth slowdown as higher prices for gasoline, diesel fuel and other energy products weigh on activity.
  • And that's giving the Federal Reserve more breathing room to avoid rate hikes.

Of note: This inversion of the relationship is clearly on the mind of the Fed's leadership, even if they aren't ready to draw firm conclusions about its implications.

  • In his news conference two weeks ago, chairman Kevin Warsh pointed to "a stable correlation" between oil prices and interest rates for much of this year, and while noting that he is not the author of a Wall Street newsletter, he nonetheless mused on the relationship at some length.

What they're saying: "That correlation has been quite strong, until very recently where you've seen oil prices continue to move up, largely due to geopolitical events," he said. "But what's happened? Interest rates have rolled over to the downside."

  • "To the extent that oil prices were to move lower, again, probably due to geopolitical events, that's something that we're going to have to interrogate. What are the effects on the Fed's dual mandate? What are the effects on financial market prices, and what are we going to do about it?"
  • "But that's a hypothetical, and in fact, if we look at financial market prices, futures prices for oil, they've moved up over the course of the last several weeks, and I can't help but take note of that too."

The bottom line: If this macro regime change persists, it suggests the Fed has more leeway to move with caution on further rate hikes, no matter what happens in the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Elon Musk's empire braces for Democratic crackdown
item.description:
Elon Musk's sprawling empire — from rockets to robots, electric cars to AI — is facing a political onslaught with few parallels in modern corporate history.

Why it matters: The world's richest man confronts a constellation of risks spanning the halls of Congress, his Texas industrial empire, Wall Street and his vision for AI supremacy.

💰 Political: To Democrats, Musk embodies corrosive forces of the MAGA era — extreme wealth, billionaire influence over government, the gutting of federal institutions, the poisoning of social media and the unchecked power of AI.

  • Musk spent at least $475 million on the midterms, becoming the election's largest individual donor — only to see more than 99% of his traceable spending go to losing candidates, according to WIRED.

Musk's most humiliating defeat came in Texas, where a $160 million bet on Ken Paxton ended in a Democratic sweep of the Senate seat, governorship and attorney general's office.

  • In a hint of a possible détente, Sen.-elect James Talarico praised the billionaire as a "great business leader and entrepreneur," and offered to work with him on technology and innovation. Musk, who said last month that Talarico "hates Texas," responded: "Nice of him to say that."

⚖️ Congressional: Armed with subpoena power, Democrats are preparing to investigate Musk's DOGE operation, its access to sensitive government data and whether his companies benefited from his extraordinary influence over the Trump administration.

  • Musk is already downplaying his dependence on Washington, claiming government contracts will account for less than 5% of SpaceX revenue a year from now. "Happy to cancel any that the government doesn't want," he posted Friday.
  • The scrutiny also extends to national security: Lawmakers are demanding answers about Musk's reported communications with Vladimir Putin and his role in the October slowdown of Starshield that disrupted Ukraine's drone operations.
Elon Musk responds to reporting about his vulnerabilities in Texas. Screenshot via X

🏭 Regulatory: Musk moved his home and the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas, betting on a safe haven for his expanding empire. Now, the Democratic takeover threatens to turn his political sanctuary into a regulatory minefield.

  • Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is suing to uncover 1,374 pages of largely redacted communications with Greg Abbott, while incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has pledged to scrutinize state broadband grants awarded to Starlink.
  • Tesla's robotaxi ambitions also face new obstacles as Democrats threaten to derail federal legislation that eases state safety restrictions. Hinojosa herself urged Tesla last year to delay its Austin launch until stronger regulations took effect.

📉 Financial: Tesla and SpaceX shed roughly $460 billion in combined market value in the two days after the election, then rebounded Friday as investors raced to reassess the risks to Musk's business empire.

  • Wall Street is especially concerned that Democratic scrutiny could complicate a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger, while new restrictions on AI data centers threaten a cornerstone of Musk's growth strategy.
  • In a fitting coda to a brutal week, Musk announced Friday that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production by mid-2027, pulling the plug on a pet project plagued by weak sales, recalls and quality problems.

🤖 Technological: The midterms have given the backlash against AI new political muscle, threatening both the massive data centers powering Musk's ambitions and the technology behind Grok itself.

  • Democrats are preparing legislation that would require independent safety testing of advanced AI models and hold developers liable for harmful outputs. Lawmakers have already demanded SpaceX's AI safety records.
  • Voters sided against data-center development in 44 of 45 local referendums, while incoming Democratic governors in Georgia and Ohio pledged tougher restrictions. Musk joked on X: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."

The bottom line: Democrats must find a way to separate Musk the political combatant from Musk the industrialist, whose companies are central to America's technological and military power.

item.title: Planet-sized problems collide in permitting debate
item.description:
Efforts to fight climate change, conserve nature and build clean energy have long unfolded on competing tracks. Now, they're colliding — and exposing tough trade-offs for environmentalists.

Why it matters: Congress' sweeping permitting debate is forcing those competing priorities into the same conversation, with major consequences for climate action and conservation.

Driving the news: The Senate is set to hold an initial procedural vote Monday on a sprawling bipartisan bill that would make it easier to build power lines and energy projects of all kinds, including clean energy and fossil fuels.

  • At the heart of the debate is how much public scrutiny projects should face before they're approved — and how much protection those approvals should receive afterward.
  • Supporters say the current system takes too long, delaying clean energy and other infrastructure. Opponents warn that speeding things up could come at the expense of wildlife, public lands and tribal rights.

Between the lines: The dilemma reflects a fundamental tension within the environmental movement: Building the infrastructure needed to combat climate change can threaten nature, while protecting nature can complicate efforts to build that infrastructure.

  • Wind and solar farms, for example, can require large expanses of land, potentially disrupting wildlife habitats even as they help reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
  • "The part of my organization that cares about climate sees great opportunity and the part that cares about nature sees some dangers," said a leader of one organization that focuses on both causes, speaking anonymously to discuss the proposal candidly.

The big picture: Both parties broadly agree Washington needs to overhaul federal permitting, a perennial goal that has eluded Congress for years. The question is what reforms can attract enough support to pass both chambers.

  • The bill's bipartisan sponsors and the White House want action before year's end. But some Democrats, emboldened by their midterm victories, argue they should wait until next year, when they'll have more power and time to scrutinize the legislation.
  • Even if the Senate passes the bill, the House would still need to approve it before it could reach President Trump's desk.

Zoom out: The legislation is confined to the United States, but the tensions it exposes are global — and are playing out at two major international gatherings.

  • Representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for annual United Nations climate talks beginning Monday. The host country is pushing to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035, which would require much of the same buildout under discussion in Washington.
  • A separate, lower-profile UN gathering focused on protecting biodiversity concluded in Armenia late last month. Countries acknowledged they're falling short of their goal to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030, while agreeing on steps to accelerate progress.

What they're saying: The fact that these two discussions take place separately is part of the problem, said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute.

  • Within the U.S., the permitting debate is forcing these conversations to converge.
  • "We want everyone to be more overt about this tension, rather than covert about it," said Dasgupta, a former World Bank official. "I don't think it helps to say we can't build anything today, and also that we need to take everyone's rights away to build stuff."

Friction point: Three provisions of the Senate bill show what's at stake for conservationists.

  • Public lands: Former Biden climate adviser John Podesta warned that an earlier version of the bill could make federal permits harder for agencies to reverse, potentially allowing the Trump administration to approve development on sensitive public lands that future administrations would struggle to undo.
  • Federal reviews: The legislation would shorten and limit aspects of federal environmental reviews, including public input and opportunities to challenge project approvals in court. Conservationists and tribal organizations warn the changes could weaken protections for wildlife, public lands and culturally significant sites.
  • Wildlife: The bill would allow states to take over certain federal responsibilities for assessing how projects affect endangered species. Environmental advocates warn the changes could weaken protections for vulnerable wildlife.

Catch up quick: An updated version released Saturday revises rules on permit reversals and adds safeguards for wildlife and tribal consultation.

  • But the changes haven't satisfied all conservationists. The Wilderness Society reaffirmed its opposition on Saturday, warning the bill still threatens public lands and weakens environmental protections.

Zoom in: Carter Roberts, head of the World Wildlife Fund, which has not taken a public position on the bill, says environmentalists should seek solutions that address both climate change and nature loss.

  • "The best solutions to climate change also conserve nature and prevent it from disappearing," Roberts said.

The other side: Sponsors of the legislation and other proponents emphasize that no bill is perfect and trade-offs are inevitable.

  • "There's no question that making the system more efficient diminishes certain aspects of access to project approval. That is the point of the legislation," said Jason Grumet, head of the American Clean Power Association.
  • But he added: "We think the balance has been struck in a way that sustains meaningful access."

What we're watching: Whether lawmakers can reconcile these competing priorities and pass the bill before the new Congress takes office remains uncertain.

The bottom line: "The permitting bill debate is not a unique debate," said Dasgupta, who is in Turkey for the climate talks. "Everywhere in the world, we need to build stuff."

item.title: AI's "too big to fail" CEO is facing a crisis with no backup
item.description:
There is no Nvidia — nor an AI boom as we know it — without Jensen Huang. He has reassured jittery markets with his words, bankrolled a trillion-dollar buildout and put economies on his shoulders.

  • Now, the world is wondering if he can save himself.

Why it matters: Global markets must confront a terrifying reality: The AI ecosystem's first "too big to fail" executive is suddenly vulnerable, and there is no backup plan if he is forced to step down.

Catch up quick: Huang apologized Sunday and Nvidia's board launched an independent probe after he admitted to having a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese operative.

  • Nvidia's board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
  • President Trump stood by Huang, calling him "an honorable guy."

The big picture: Keeping his job is one thing. Maintaining the ability to steady markets, finance customers and shape government policy is another.

These are the five questions that now loom over the AI boom:

1. What happens to Nvidia? Forged 33 years ago (initially using a Denny's as an impromptu office), Nvidia is a uniquely founder-driven company, making any potential leadership transition incredibly perilous. Investors have little precedent for valuing the company without him.

  • "It's very hard to envision Nvidia run by anybody else," said Dan Gallagher, an analyst with Washington Post Intelligence and long a keen observer of the chip titan.
  • Huang has more than 60 direct reports, eschews traditional corporate layers and hasn't been publicly grooming a successor. "I don't know if anyone's going to know how to value Nvidia" without him, Gallagher told Axios.

2. What happens to the market? Huang has repeatedly rescued the AI trade from bearish sentiment.

  • On multiple occasions, he has offered backstops to shore up growth plans for companies across the AI landscape, from CoreWeave to OpenAI.
  • In July, he argued that cheaper open models would boost demand for Nvidia's chips, pushing back against a market scare.
  • Last month, he toured Europe pitching national AI projects as debt investors signaled their appetite for some AI financing was limited.

3. What happens to the companies that depend on him? The risks vary across an industry that relies on Nvidia for chips, capital and credibility.

  • The AI giants: Anthropic and OpenAI have options. Anthropic plans to barrel ahead with an IPO this month and already uses chips from Google and Amazon. OpenAI is developing its own chips in-house and with Broadcom. Diversification is underway, but replacing Nvidia is not in the cards near term.
  • The "neoclouds": Companies such as CoreWeave that rent out computing power have less room to maneuver. CoreWeave suffered a prolonged stock-and-bond selloff last month as investors began to question how it would finance continued growth. Nvidia has provided crucial backstops to many neocloud companies.
  • The "neolabs" and AI startups: Nvidia has supplied investment and offered access to computing for AI startups such as Thinking Machines Lab, as well as dozens of other startups providing a variety of services in the AI race.

4. Where does the investigation lead? Southeast Asia's data center boom puts the limits of U.S. chip restrictions in focus.

  • The loophole: U.S. restrictions on shipping advanced chips to China generally haven't stopped Chinese companies from accessing them in overseas data centers, the New York Times reported. Nvidia told the Times that remote access is consistent with U.S. export controls because the chips remain outside restricted countries.
  • That access is distinct from suspected smuggling. The Times reported that Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang worked, was under investigation for steering advanced chips to China.

5. What happens to Huang's advocacy? His arguments for selling chips to China and embracing open AI models will face renewed scrutiny, with many of his comments potentially being seen in a new light due to the relationship.

  • Huang has repeatedly, and stridently, pushed to loosen restrictions on sales to China, arguing that reliance on American technology serves U.S. interests.

The bottom line: Huang has made himself the AI boom's indispensable man.

  • The industry must now reckon with what happens when its fortunes depend so heavily on his.

item.title: Jensen Huang spy scandal rocks AI race
item.description:
The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence.

Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House.

  • Trump stood by Huang on Sunday evening, telling reporters that the Nvidia CEO is "an honorable guy" and "probably has an excuse" for his infidelity.

The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice.

  • He has brushed aside fears of both a speculative bubble and technological catastrophe, joining forces with Trump to calm markets and the public as warnings of an AI apocalypse reached fever pitch.
  • For almost any other CEO, an affair with a suspected foreign intelligence operative could be career-ending. Huang's grip on Nvidia — and the company's extraordinary importance to the AI economy — may insulate him from the same fate.

Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation.

  • U.S. officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited by Beijing's top spy agency to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia's campaign to expand advanced chip sales to China.
  • Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Jensen Huang, who intends to remain CEO during the investigation.

Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO.

  • The company portrayed their interactions as routine business dealings — an account now under scrutiny in the wake of Huang's admission that he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
  • Trump defended Huang on Oct. 31 as a "great, brilliant person," but hedged when asked if he should remain a White House adviser: "I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary."

The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public.

  • Trump was briefed in 2025, according to the Times, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally oversaw a classified intelligence memo warning senior officials this spring.
  • Yet Trump continued to embrace Huang as a trusted adviser, welcoming him to the White House as the Nvidia chief pressed to loosen restrictions on advanced chip exports to China.

Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia.

  • "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications, said in a statement.

What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight.

  • A post-election rout wiped trillions from U.S. stocks on Thursday, deepening uncertainty over an AI boom that has powered much of the market's growth.
  • Huang's admission is now poised to open an explosive new line of inquiry: Did the White House disregard intelligence warnings while advancing policies championed by one of Trump's closest corporate allies?

item.title: Trump backs Nvidia's Huang amid affair, spy investigation
item.description:
President Trump defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday night, even as the company's board launched an investigation into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Why it matters: The blowback to Huang's relationship is only getting more intense by the hour, with multiple members of Congress calling for probes and investors saying the news could put a cloud over the entire AI trade.

What they're saying: Trump was asked Sunday night if he's taking Huang with him on an Asia trip next week.

  • "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him," the president told reporters.
  • "I haven't heard that he's done anything wrong," Trump added. "He dealt with somebody but, you know, so does everybody else."

The intrigue: The New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed earlier this year about Huang's relationship with the potential spy but chose not to act.

  • Huang has been one of Trump's favorite corporate executives since his return to office, with Huang frequently appearing at White House events.
  • He also traveled with Trump to China earlier this year, even after the reported memo warning the president of Huang's relationship.

What's next: A group of House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to agree by Nov. 11 to a date for a briefing on his relationship and Nvidia's national security controls.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy in a message to his company, and the company's board announced an independent investigation Sunday.

Why it matters: The scandal raises national security concerns involving one of the world's most powerful tech CEOs, who has pushed to loosen restrictions on selling advanced AI chips to China amid the two countries' race for technological dominance.

Driving the news: "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios.

  • "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did."
  • Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.
  • "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

Meanwhile: Nvidia's board said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter.

  • The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership.

Zoom out: Huang has been a key voice in Washington pushing to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China.

  • He argued that keeping American technology in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and prevented China from developing their own potentially more advanced chips.

Flashback: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned top Trump officials about Huang's relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believed was a Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Friday.

  • The woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to seek information and potentially push for Nvidia's advanced chips to be made available in China, countering existing restrictions, the Times reported.

What they're saying: "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications at Nvidia said in a statement.

item.title: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing increasing congressional scrutiny after multiple reports Friday night suggested he had a romantic relationship with a purported Chinese spy.

Why it matters: Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO, the man who runs one of the world's largest companies and whose products are central to the world's most important technology.

  • The mere suggestion that he was in some way compromised by a Chinese intelligence agent could quickly become a major, bipartisan focus of the incoming Congress.

What they're saying: Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) promised a probe of the latest Times report and Huang's relationships.

  • "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers," Coons posted to X, linking in another post to the Times' story.

Catch up quick: A series of reports over the last 10 days has raised concerns about an allegedly illicit relationship with an undercurrent of espionage.

  • Oct. 29: The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang and a tech executive named Alice Huang had a "close relationship," that U.S. authorities had concerns about her intelligence connections with China, and that President Trump had been briefed on the situation.
  • Oct. 31: The Wall Street Journal reported that intelligence authorities in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan all had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy.
  • Nov. 5: A group of House Republican committee chairs asked Jensen Huang to give them a briefing on his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's controls over sensitive information, saying they need to determine "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."
  • Nov. 6: Both the New York Times and Financial Times reported that Alice Huang was in fact a Chinese spy, recruited by top intelligence officials specifically to spy on Jensen Huang. Her purported goal: to convince him to lobby U.S. officials to allow chip exports to China.
  • The FT also reported that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang had a romantic relationship.

For the record: Nvidia has repeatedly and firmly denied that Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang was anything but a typical business contact, and insisted that no sensitive information would have been shared with her or anyone else.

  • The company did not respond to Axios's request for comment on Saturday.
  • The Chinese government has also publicly denied engaging with Alice Huang to spy on Jensen Huang.

The big picture: President Trump and his administration have staked the country's future on beating China in the race to develop and control advanced AI.

  • Nvidia's chips are central to that vision, and Jensen Huang has been close to Trump throughout this term.
  • There've been back-and-forth fights over whether Nvidia's chips can be sold to China or not, but also extensive reporting that those chips are making their way to Chinese companies regardless.

What's next: The Republican chairmen who requested a briefing from Jensen Huang gave him a Nov. 11 deadline to set a date for their meeting.
